lead: LPI's entry-level Linux cert. It proves you can work at the Linux command line: move around the file system, handle files and permissions, read logs, write a short script and log in over SSH. Most SOC tools and servers run Linux, so this is skill you'll use every day.
objSub: Both versions earn the same certificate. Version 2.0 is current; 1.6 stays open until April 2027. Pick the one you'll test on, then tick objectives as you study. Progress saves on this device.

v20.label: Ver 2.0
v20.note: The new version. It adds systemd services, journalctl, SSH keys, sudo, and Linux in VMs and the cloud, and drops old tools like ifconfig and netstat. Study this one unless you already prepared for 1.6. At launch it's in English; LPI says French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese and Spanish follow within a few months.
v20.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 2.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 40 questions it gets (shown at the start of each line). The bars show each topic's share.

domains.name: The Linux Operating System and Open Source Software
obj: Linux Distributions
Weight 2. Kernel vs userspace, distro families (Debian, Enterprise Linux, SUSE, Alpine), release types like LTS, stable and rolling, and how Android relates to Linux.
Major Open Source Applications
Weight 2. Common desktop, web and server apps (Firefox, LibreOffice, Apache, NGINX, PostgreSQL, Samba), languages like Python and C, and package tools: apt, dnf, zypper, apk.
Open Source Software and Licensing
Weight 1. Free and open source ideas, copyleft (GPL) vs permissive (BSD) licenses, Creative Commons, the FSF and OSI.
Linux Usage
Weight 2. Where Linux runs (desktops, servers, VMs, cloud, embedded), the vi and nano editors, and safe habits: strong passwords, password managers, MFA, passkeys, HTTPS, careful USB use.

domains.name: Command Line Basics
obj: Command Line Usage
Weight 3. Bash syntax, variables, quoting, echo, history, PATH and export, and how a built-in differs from a program (type).
Documentation, Man Pages and Usage Information
Weight 2. man pages, -h and --help, and the docs in /usr/share/doc.
Files, Directories and Paths
Weight 2. ls and its options, cd, absolute vs relative paths, . and .., ~, hidden files, and finding files by name with find.
File and Directory Management
Weight 2. cp, mv, rm, touch, mkdir, rmdir, case sensitivity and simple wildcards (globbing).

domains.name: Data Processing
obj: File Archives and Compression
Weight 2. Create, list and extract tar and zip archives; gzip, bzip2 and xz.
Redirections and String Processing
Weight 3. Pipes, input and output redirection, and filtering text with grep (and grep -E), less, cat, head, tail, sort, uniq, cut and wc.
Shell Scripting Basics
Weight 4, the heaviest single objective. Scripts with #!/bin/bash, variables, arguments, if tests on files and variables, for loops over lists and wildcards, and exit status.

domains.name: Linux System Administration Basics
obj: Linux Installation and Provisioning
Weight 1. Installing on hardware, VMs and cloud instances; ISO files and images; dual boot; Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).
Computer Hardware and Device Access
Weight 2. CPUs (x86, ARM), storage, NICs, drivers and kernel modules, device files in /dev, plus /boot, /sys, /dev/null, /dev/zero and /dev/urandom.
Processes and Log Messages
Weight 3. ps, top and free; start, stop and check services with systemctl; read logs with journalctl, dmesg and /var/log; /proc and /etc.
Network Configuration
Weight 2. IPv4 and IPv6 basics, routes, DNS, ip addr and ip route, ss, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf, resolvectl, DHCP and SLAAC, ping and host.

domains.name: Security and File System Permissions
obj: Remote Logins, File Transfers and Elevated Permissions
Weight 2. Root, standard and system users; sudo and su; ssh, scp, ssh-keygen and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
User and Group Management
Weight 2. /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/skel; useradd, groupadd and passwd; who's logged in with id, w and last.
File System Permissions and Ownership
Weight 2. Read ls -l, change permissions with chmod and ownership with chown.
Special Directories and Files
Weight 1. /tmp and /var/tmp, the sticky bit, and symbolic links with ln -s.

extras.title: Commands to know
rows: Every file, hidden ones too, with permissions and owners
cd .. goes up one level; pwd prints where you are
Copy · move or rename · delete (there's no recycle bin)
Lines that match. -i ignores case, -E allows extended patterns
First or last lines. tail -f keeps following a log
sort | uniq -c counts repeats. Sort first: uniq only merges neighbors

journalctl -u sshd: log entries for one service
ip addr shows addresses; ip route shows routes and the gateway
ssh logs in · scp copies files · ssh-keygen makes a key pair

Run a file · enter a directory

method: Use the five topics above as your checklist. Scripting (013.3) carries the most weight of any single objective.
Read LPI's free Learning Materials for each objective. They're written by LPI and follow the objectives exactly.
Type every command yourself in WSL or a VM. Linux sticks when your fingers know it, not just your eyes.
Flashcards for commands and options, permission numbers, and where files live.
Timed 40-question sets in 60 minutes. Review every miss and run the command to see why.
tips: Questions often turn on one flag: -r, -f, -l, -i. Know what the common ones do.
When a question shows ls -l or ps output, the answer is usually in one column.
2>&1 and > in the wrong order give a different result. Practice redirection until it's automatic.
There's no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

quiz.code:
#!/bin/bash
for f in /var/log/*.log; do
  if [ -s "$f" ]; then echo "$f"; fi
done
o: The name of every .log file in /var/log that is not empty
Right. The loop walks the matching files, and -s is true when a file exists and its size is greater than zero.
The name of every empty .log file in /var/log
That would be ! -s. The -s test is true for files that have data.
Every .log file in /var/log and all of its subdirectories
The wildcard only matches files directly in /var/log. It doesn't search subdirectories.
The first non-empty .log file, then it stops
Nothing ends the loop early, so every matching file is checked.

quiz.q: failed.txt has one IP address per line, one line per failed SSH login. Which pipeline shows the 5 addresses with the MOST failures?
o: sort failed.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5
Right. sort groups identical lines, uniq -c counts each group, sort -nr puts the biggest counts first, and head keeps the top 5.
uniq -c failed.txt | sort -nr | head -5
uniq only merges lines that are next to each other. Without sorting first, the same IP gets counted in many separate pieces.
sort -u failed.txt | head -5
-u removes duplicates, so you lose the counts. You'd just get the first 5 addresses in order.
sort failed.txt | uniq | wc -l
That counts how many different addresses there are, not which ones failed most.

quiz.q: Which command saves the list of .conf files to found.txt and throws away the “Permission denied” errors?
o: find / -name "*.conf" > found.txt 2>/dev/null
Right. > sends normal output to the file and 2>/dev/null discards the error stream.
find / -name "*.conf" 2> found.txt
That saves only the errors to the file. The results still print on screen.
find / -name "*.conf" > found.txt 2>&1
2>&1 sends the errors into found.txt as well, mixed in with the results.
find / -name "*.conf" | tee found.txt
tee saves the results, but the errors still print on screen. Pipes carry only normal output.

quiz.q: You're handed evidence.tar.gz. You want to see what's inside WITHOUT extracting or changing it. Which command?
o: tar -tzf evidence.tar.gz
Right. -t lists the contents, -z handles gzip and -f names the file. Nothing is written to disk.
tar -xzf evidence.tar.gz
-x extracts everything into the current directory, which is what you wanted to avoid.
tar -czf evidence.tar.gz
-c creates an archive. Run like this, it would try to overwrite the evidence file.
gzip -d evidence.tar.gz
That decompresses the file and replaces it with evidence.tar, so the original is changed.

quiz.q: User jdoe is in the soc group but isn't root. What can jdoe do with triage.sh?
quiz.code:
$ ls -l triage.sh
-rwxr-x--- 1 root soc 812 Nov  9 08:14 triage.sh
o: Read and run it, but not change it
Right. The middle set (r-x) applies to the soc group: read and execute, no write.
Nothing at all
The last set (---) is for everyone else. jdoe is in the group, so the group set applies.
Read it only
The group set also has x, so jdoe can run it.
Read, change and run it
Only the owner (root) has w. The group set has no write permission.

quiz.q: A file holds an API key. The owner must read and write it, and nobody else should have any access. Which command fits BEST?
o: chmod 600 apikey.txt
Right. 6 (4+2) gives the owner read and write; 0 and 0 give the group and others nothing.
chmod 700 apikey.txt
It blocks everyone else, but it also makes the file executable, which a key file doesn't need.
chmod 644 apikey.txt
644 lets the group and everyone else read the key.
chmod 666 apikey.txt
666 lets every user on the system read and change it.

quiz.q: You made a key pair with ssh-keygen on your laptop so you can log in to server1 without a password. What goes where?
o: The public key (.pub) goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on server1; the private key stays on your laptop
Right. The server checks your login against the public keys in authorized_keys. The private key never leaves your machine.
The private key goes into authorized_keys on server1
Never copy the private key anywhere. Anyone who has it can log in as you.
The public key goes into known_hosts on your laptop
known_hosts stores the SERVERS' host keys so your laptop can spot an impostor. It doesn't log you in.
Both keys go into /etc/ssh on server1
/etc/ssh holds the server's own host keys and settings, not user login keys.

quiz.q: The SSH service on a server stopped answering. Which ONE command shows whether it's running AND its most recent log lines?
o: systemctl status sshd
Right. It shows active or failed, the main PID, and the last several journal lines for the unit.
journalctl -u sshd
It shows the service's logs, but not whether it's running right now.
systemctl start sshd
That tries to start it. It doesn't tell you what went wrong.
ps aux
It lists processes, but shows no service state and no logs.

quiz.q: A Linux host can ping 8.8.8.8, but ping intranet.example.com fails with “Name or service not known.” What should you check first?
o: The DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf (or with resolvectl)
Right. Reaching an outside IP proves addressing and routing work. Only name lookups fail, so look at DNS.
The default route with ip route show
Traffic already reaches 8.8.8.8, so the default route works.
The machine's own name in /etc/hostname
That's this machine's name. It doesn't affect looking up other names.
The network card driver
A driver problem would stop the ping to 8.8.8.8 too.

quiz.q: Which directory holds live, kernel-generated information about running processes, like /…/1234/status for PID 1234?
o: /proc
Right. /proc is a virtual file system the kernel builds on the fly. Every running process gets a numbered directory.
/dev
/dev holds device files such as disks and terminals.
/var/log
/var/log holds log files that services write. It isn't live process state.
/boot
/boot holds the kernel and boot loader files.

quiz.q: You're in /home/analyst/cases. Which command takes you to /home/analyst/tools?
o: cd ../tools
Right. .. goes up to /home/analyst, then into tools.
cd /tools
The leading / makes it absolute: it looks for /tools at the top of the file system.
cd ./tools
./ means inside the current directory, so it looks for /home/analyst/cases/tools.
cd ~tools
~tools means the home directory of a user named tools.

quiz.q: You type scan and get “command not found.” The program is /opt/tools/scan and it IS executable. What's the cause?
o: /opt/tools isn't in your PATH. Run /opt/tools/scan or add it with export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools
Right. The shell only searches the directories listed in PATH for bare command names.
You need to run it with sudo
sudo changes who runs it, not where the shell looks. You'd get the same error.
It needs chmod +x
It's already executable. The shell simply can't find it.
Its man page is missing
Man pages are only documentation. They don't affect running a program.

quiz.q: Your team changes a GPL-licensed tool and gives the changed version to other units. What does the GPL require?
o: Make the source code of your changed version available under the GPL too
Right. The GPL is copyleft: if you distribute a modified version, its source must go along under the same license.
Nothing, as long as you don't charge for it
The GPL's terms apply when you distribute, whether you charge or not.
You may keep your changes private and relicense the tool
That's allowed by permissive licenses like BSD, not by the GPL.
Pay a license fee to the Free Software Foundation
The GPL doesn't charge fees. The FSF wrote the license; it doesn't sell it.

pbqs.title: Pick the command for each task
pbqs.scenario: You're on shift with a Linux terminal open. Pick the command that does each task. Each answer is used once; three are distractors.

items.text: Watch /var/log/auth.log and see new lines the moment they're written.
items.why: tail -f keeps the file open and prints new lines as they arrive.

items.text: Search /home for every file whose name ends in .sh.
items.why: find /home -name "*.sh" walks the directory tree and matches names. (locate was dropped from the 2.0 objectives and relies on a database that may be stale.)

items.text: Count how many lines are in users.txt.
Show only the lines in auth.log that contain “Failed password.”
items.why: grep prints the lines that match a pattern.

items.text: See which processes are using the most CPU right now, updating live.
items.why: top shows a live, sorted view of processes and resource use.

items.text: Check your user ID and every group you belong to.
items.why: id prints your UID, primary group and every group membership.

items.text: Read the full manual for chmod.
items.why: man chmod opens the manual page.

pbqs.title: Set the right permissions
pbqs.scenario: For each file or directory, pick the chmod number and the matching ls -l permission string.

rows.req: A private SSH key: only the owner can read and write it.
rows.why: 600 shows as rw------- in ls -l. SSH refuses to use a private key that other users can read.

rows.req: A team script: the owner has full control, the group can read and run it, others get nothing.
rows.why: 750 shows as rwxr-x---. 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x, 0 is nothing.

rows.req: A web page: everyone can read it, only the owner can change it.
rows.why: 644 shows as rw-r--r--, the normal setting for files.

rows.req: A case directory: the owner and the soc group can do everything in it, nobody else can enter.
rows.why: 770 shows as rwxrwx---. A directory needs x before anyone can enter it.

rows.req: An evidence file: the owner and group can read it, nobody can change it.
rows.why: 440 shows as r--r-----. Read-only for owner and group helps prevent accidental edits.

rows.req: A tool every user can run, but only the owner can change.
rows.why: 755 shows as rwxr-xr-x, the normal setting for programs.

pbqs.title: Read the Linux logs
pbqs.scenario: These lines came from journalctl and /var/log on a server you're watching. Pick what each one shows. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.log:
sshd[2231]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51122 ssh2
sshd[2231]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51130 ssh2
sshd[2231]: message repeated 38 times
items.why: Many failed logins for a user that doesn't exist, from one outside address, is password guessing (brute force).

items.log: sshd[3310]: Accepted publickey for analyst from 10.4.2.15 port 50544 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:q8V2...
items.why: “Accepted publickey” means the login used an SSH key, not a password.

items.log: sudo: jdoe : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/jdoe ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/cat /etc/shadow
items.why: jdoe ran a command as root through sudo, here reading the password hash file. Worth asking why.

items.log: useradd[4102]: new user: name=svc_backup, UID=1005, GID=1005, home=/home/svc_backup, shell=/bin/bash
items.why: useradd logged a new account. An unexpected new account with a login shell is a classic persistence sign.

items.log:
systemd[1]: nginx.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
systemd[1]: nginx.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
items.why: systemd reports the service's main process exited with an error. Check systemctl status nginx and its config.

items.log:
usb 1-2: new high-speed USB device number 7 using xhci_hcd
usb-storage 1-2:1.0: USB Mass Storage device detected
items.why: The kernel detected a USB mass storage device. Many units restrict removable media, so this may need a report.
